english.html: At the beginning of this discourse several examples of likenesses were recited <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>; besides which, since the subject presents itself, Gnaeus Pompeius, afterwards called Strabo, father of the great Pompey, had a cook named Menogenes, who, because he squinted, was called by the surname Strabo, and who so vividly resembled his master that in the end the master, by the voice of the people, took on the surname of his cook, and was called Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo, that is to say, the Squinter <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>. Likewise we read also that Publius Cornelius Lentulus and Quintus Metellus Nepos, being Consuls of Rome in the year 697 from the founding of Rome, were so like two players of comedy — of whom the one was named Spinther, resembling Lentulus, and the other Pamphilus, resembling Metellus — that in the end Lentulus was surnamed Spinther; and Metellus likewise would have taken the surname of Pamphilus, had the surname of Pius not been given him beforehand <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>.

notes.gloss: The catalogue of doubles: Vibius and Publicius, Scipio and Serapion, Hybreas, Toranius's twins, Sura's fisherman, and the rest.

notes.citation: Pliny, Natural History VII.10 (§54; c. 12 in the old chapter division)
notes.original: Pline au liu. vij. c. xij.
notes.gloss: Pliny: Pompey's father exchanged his name for that of his cook Menogenes, whose squint he shared; cf. Valerius Maximus IX.14.2.

notes.citation: Pliny, Natural History VII.10 (§54) again, as printed
notes.original: Pline aud. lib. vij. c. xij.
notes.gloss: Aud. = au d[it], "in the said book". Pliny: Lentulus and Metellus Nepos, consuls together, were surnamed from the actors Spinther and Pamphilus; cf. Valerius Maximus IX.14.4.

english.html: It is easy also to answer the point that the said de Rols, confronted with the accused, refused to swear; for that can change nothing of the truth.

The saying of the Philosopher, renewed in our laws, is that for our affirming or denying, the truth changes not at all <sup class="mk" data-key="a2">a2</sup>; which, as Cicero says in a certain place, has always had such power that by any art, device or contrivance of man whatsoever it has never been able to be overturned; and though it have no protector to take up its defence, it defends itself well enough of itself <sup class="mk" data-key="b2">b2</sup>. And in another place: O how great, says he, is the force of truth, which against the wit, ruses and wiles of man defends itself easily, without the help or succour of any other <sup class="mk" data-key="c2">c2</sup>.

notes.citation: Digest 50.1 (Ad municipalem et de incolis), l. Adsumptio (D. 50.1.6 pr., Ulpian)
notes.gloss: Adsumptio originis, quae non est, veritati non praeiudicat — "the assumption of an origin one does not have does not prejudice the truth: for no one by lying makes himself of no origin, nor by claiming another's origin acquires it."

notes.citation: Cicero, In Vatinium (the passage on the power of truth has not been located in the speech as it survives; section unverified)
notes.original: Ciceron en l'oraiſon con tre vatin.
notes.gloss: Coras's paraphrase — truth never overturned by human art, and defending itself without a protector — is close to the Pro Caelio passage cited next; whether he has a distinct In Vatinium sentence in mind could not be confirmed.

notes.original: Ciceron en l'oraiſon pro M. Cœlio.
notes.gloss: O magnam vim veritatis, quae contra hominum ingenia, calliditatem, sollertiam contraque fictas omnium insidias facile se per se ipsa defendat! — "O great power of truth, which against the wit, cunning and cleverness of men, and against the feigned snares of all, easily defends itself by itself."

lines: ſe pourroyent citer pluſieurs exemples.
Au commencement de ce diſcours ont eſté recitez
pluſieurs exẽples des ſimilitudes {a}. outre leſquels, puis
que le propos ſe preſente, Cn. Pompee, depuis appelé
Strabo, pere du grand Pompee, auoit vn cuyſinier, nõ-
mé Menogenes, lequel par ce qu'il eſtoit louſche, on
l'appeloit de ſurnom Strabo, ſi viuement reſſemblant
ſõ maiſtre, qu'en fin le maiſtre, par la voix du peuple, ap-
porta le ſurnom de ſon cuiſinier, & fut appelé Cn. Pom-
pee Strabõ. c'eſt à dire le Bigle {b}. De meſmes nous liſons
auſſi, Publius Cornelius Lentulus, & Quintus Metel-
lus Nepos, eſtans Conſuls de Rome, en l'annee 697.
de Rome baſtie: furent ſi ſemblables à deux iouëurs
de comedie, deſquels l'vn ſe nommoit Spynther, ſem-
blable à Lentule: & l'autre Pamphyle, ſemblable à Me-
telle: qu'en fin Lentule fut ſurnõmé Spynther: & Metel-
le pareillement euſt prins le ſurnom de Pamphyle, ſi
au parauant ne luy euſt eſté donné le ſurnom de Pie {c}.
Il eſt aiſé auſsi de reſpondre, à ce que
ladite de Rols confrontee au preuenu,
refuſa iurer, car cela ne peut changer rien
de la verité.
La ſentence du Philoſophe, refriquee en nos loix
eſt, que pour noſtre affermer, ou nier, la verité ne ſe
change point {a2}. laquelle comme dit en quelque lieu
Ciceron, a eu touſiours tant de puiſſance, que par art,
engin, ou machine quelconques d'homme, elle n'ha peu
eſtre rẽuerſee, & bien qu'elle n'aye aucun protecteur,
qui prenne ſa defenſe, elle ſe defend aſſez de ſoy-meſme
{b2}. Et en autre lieu, O que la force de la verité dit il, eſt
grande, laquelle contre l'eſperit, ruſes, & cauteles
de l'homme ſe defend aiſeement, ſans aide ni ſecours
d'autruy {c2}.
